# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, affecting more than 64 million people worldwide and accounting for substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure [1]. Despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and device-based interventions such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), a large proportion of patients remain symptomatic [2]. Importantly, CRT is only beneficial in patients with prolonged QRS duration, leaving a substantial population with narrow QRS complexes without an effective device option [3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) therapy has emerged as a non-excitatory electrical stimulation technique aimed at improving contractile function and symptoms in selected patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [4].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM delivers high-voltage, non-excitatory biphasic electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [5]. Because the signals are applied when the myocardium cannot be depolarized, they do not trigger new contractions but instead modulate the strength of existing contractions [6]. Experimental studies have demonstrated that CCM enhances myocardial calcium handling, increasing the amplitude of intracellular calcium transients [7]. At the molecular level, CCM has been shown to reverse the fetal gene program, normalize expression of key calcium-cycling proteins such as SERCA2a and phospholamban, and improve sarcoplasmic reticulum function [8,9]. These changes appear to translate into reverse remodeling at both the cellular and chamber level [10].

Additional research suggests that CCM exerts effects beyond acute inotropy, including improvements in autonomic balance and favorable modulation of myocardial gene expression associated with hypertrophy and fibrosis [11,12]. Unlike traditional positive inotropic agents, which increase myocardial oxygen consumption and worsen long-term outcomes, CCM does not appear to be associated with increased energy expenditure or arrhythmic burden [13].

## Clinical Evidence

The clinical evaluation of CCM has progressed through several randomized controlled trials. The FIX-HF-4 study, a double-blind crossover trial, demonstrated improvements in exercise tolerance and quality of life with CCM [14]. The FIX-HF-5 trial enrolled patients with NYHA class III–IV symptoms and ejection fraction ≤35% and, while it did not meet its primary composite endpoint, demonstrated improvements in anaerobic threshold and quality of life in prespecified subgroups [15]. A subsequent analysis identified that patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% derived the greatest benefit, informing the design of later trials [16].

The pivotal FIX-HF-5C study confirmed significant improvements in peak oxygen consumption, six-minute walk distance, and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire scores in patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% [17]. These findings supported regulatory approval of the Optimizer system by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2019 [18]. Pooled analyses of randomized data have suggested potential benefits on heart failure hospitalization and functional capacity [19,20].

Registry and real-world data, including the CCM-REG study, have demonstrated sustained improvements in NYHA class and quality of life, with reductions in HF hospitalizations over long-term follow-up [21,22]. Observational evidence also suggests possible benefit in patients with atrial fibrillation and in those with mildly reduced ejection fraction, populations underrepresented in earlier trials [23,24].

## Safety and Patient Selection

CCM via the Optimizer system has demonstrated an acceptable safety profile, with complication rates comparable to other implantable cardiac devices [25]. Importantly, CCM does not interfere with defibrillator function, and the two therapies can be safely combined [26]. Current candidates are typically patients with symptomatic HFrEF on optimal GDMT, NYHA class III, ejection fraction 25–45%, and a narrow QRS who are therefore ineligible for CRT [27]. Newer device iterations have reduced the number of required leads, simplifying implantation [28].

## Future Directions

Ongoing investigations are exploring the role of CCM in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), where preliminary data are encouraging [29]. Larger outcome-driven trials assessing mortality endpoints, cost-effectiveness analyses, and integration with emerging pharmacotherapies such as SGLT2 inhibitors will be essential to define the precise role of CCM in contemporary HF management [30].

## Conclusion

CCM represents a promising device-based therapy that addresses an unmet need among symptomatic HFrEF patients ineligible for CRT. Robust evidence supports improvements in exercise capacity and quality of life, with reverse remodeling demonstrated mechanistically. Further long-term and broader-population studies will help solidify its place in the HF therapeutic armamentarium.
